question: One stage of a service review is described as 'look into how customers feel about our support'. It keeps returning broad material the team cannot act on. How should the stage be redefined?
options: A) As a stage answering one question, such as which support issues drive customers to contact the team twice.
B) As two stages of the same broad description, so the material arrives in halves that are easier to read through.
C) As a stage that gathers as much material as possible on support quality, which the team then filters down itself.
D) As a stage covering customer feeling about support, pricing and product together, giving the findings context.
correct_answers: A) As a stage answering one question, such as which support issues drive customers to contact the team twice.
explanations: Correct. A stage is only well formed when it has a single answerable question and a recognisable finishing point. Naming the specific behaviour to explain gives the stage a boundary and gives the team a result they can act on.
Halving a vague stage produces two vague stages, since the problem is the absence of a specific question rather than the volume.
Collecting more of the same material moves the filtering work onto the team without making the stage's purpose any clearer.
Widening the scope makes the output broader still, and the team already cannot act on what the narrower version returns.
